title: Installing and Configuring the AWS CLI
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of installing and configuring the aws cli and its relationship to AWS CLI, SDKs, APIs, and Developer Tools.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to installing and configuring the aws cli.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn installing and configuring the aws cli in the context of AWS CLI, SDKs, APIs, and Developer Tools. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Installing and Configuring the AWS CLI matters because it is one part of aws cli, sdks and apis. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Module 4: AWS CLI, SDKs, APIs, and Developer Tools
content_blocks.alt_text: Five-step overview for module 4, AWS CLI, SDKs, APIs, and Developer Tools, followed by verification, least-privilege security, recovery, and cost-cleanup checks.
content_blocks.caption: Module 4 learning sequence: understand the concept, make a controlled design/configuration, verify behavior, and document security/reliability/cost trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Installing and Configuring the AWS CLI belongs to AWS CLI, SDKs, APIs, and Developer Tools. The console, CLI, service APIs and SDKs expose the same cloud capabilities through different interfaces. Keep credentials outside source code and prefer named profiles or role-based providers.

The PDF lists these subtopics: CLI installation; Named profiles; Credential providers; Region and output configuration. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For installing and configuring the aws cli, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: CLI installation
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: Named profiles
items.text: Document the data shape, access pattern, retention, permissions, recovery path and performance needs. Verify query or storage behavior with representative synthetic data.

items.title: Credential providers
items.text: State the principal, action, resource and applicable conditions. Prefer scoped permissions and temporary credentials, protect secrets, and collect evidence that access is both limited and usable.

items.title: Region and output configuration
items.text: Record ownership, dependencies and teardown/recovery behavior so the design can be operated safely after the first successful test.

content_blocks.title: Use an SDK credential provider: Installing and Configuring the AWS CLI
content_blocks.code:
import boto3

sts = boto3.client("sts")
identity = sts.get_caller_identity()
print(identity["Arn"])
content_blocks.expected_output: Prints the caller ARN when Boto3 can resolve valid AWS credentials and the caller has permission for sts:GetCallerIdentity.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This block is an inspectable example, not an AWS action performed by CodeLeaf. Review the example as text and adapt it only after checking current official service documentation. Do not apply/deploy changes in a real account without account-owner approval, least-privilege permissions and a reviewed cost/cleanup plan.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “Installing and Configuring the AWS CLI”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for Installing and Configuring the AWS CLI with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: Installing and Configuring the AWS CLI is taught as part of AWS CLI, SDKs, APIs, and Developer Tools.
The console, CLI, service APIs and SDKs expose the same cloud capabilities through different interfaces. Keep credentials outside source code and prefer named profiles or role-based providers.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
